From the Illustrated London News.) THE INTERNATIONAL FREE-TRADE CONGRESS. The Congress of the Association ior International Customs Reform held its first sitting last Monday morning, at the Gothic Hall of the Hotel de Ville, Brussels, and was most numerously attended ; and the more so as many members of the International Benevolent Association delayed their departure in prder to attend ; and, in so far as regards some, to give their full adhesion to the principles of practical utility and international benefit which form the basis of this praiseworthy institution. M. Scialoga (Sardinia) was the first person to ascend the tribune. He addressed the meeting at some length, describing the many reforms carried out by the Government of his country in the tariff. There was, however, a determination on the part of the people of Piedmont and other Slates to persevere in their demands for the most perfect liberty of commerce in Sardinia. Further reforms were necessary to give proper i fleet to commercial and industrial freedom. Other abuses must he swept away þÿ facilities should be given to commerce at. the various seaports þÿ kuowledge should he more generally diffused amongst the people. The honest and enlightened Monarch who uow reigned in Sardinia was determined to persevere in the promotion of ail such important subjects. His people had already tasted the sweets of liberty ; aud, in concert with their ruler, were bent on developing to the utmost the industrial, moral, intellectual, and political interests of the country.

Couut Arrivaheno ('Tuscany) next addressed the Congress in a very brief speech. Me observed that his country was the first to proclaim the freedom of commerce. He presented, on behalf of the Gaietn (lergraphilo of Florence, a paper detailing the history of commercial legisla tion in Tuscany. M. Gamier (Palis) remarked that Free-trade principles wore scarcely understood in France ten years ago, and their progress was arrested by the Revolution of lt>44. Tim Provisional Government, although professing liberal principles, shrank from proposing the admission free of duty of primary articles of subsistence. The Constituent Assembly effected nothing in the shape of commercial reform The Ministry ol December, 1852, brought forward several important reforms, and cattle was admitted free from imposts. Many other artieles were also admitted at nominal rates, to the great advantage of tinpoorer classes. A project had been submitted to the Corps LogL'.atif for the removal of all prohibitory duties, and it was to he hoped that that body would he induced to make a movement itt the rigiit direction The advocates of Freetrade were steadily increasing in France The entire press regarded it favourably. M. Wolowski (France) said that, though France did not proceed as rapidly as they could wish in the path of commercial freedom, it had nevertheless made considerable progress in that direction The principles of Free-trade had a body of illustrious champions in his country, who. bv their eloquent and logical writings, had de

monstrated that the only true bases of international commerce were harmony and mutual þÿconfidence not jealousy and antagonism. M Molinar (Belgium) described the reductions that had been made of late years in the Belgian Customs, and the further reforms that, were deemed necessary. M Pascal Duprat (Paris) passed in rapid review the various obstacles which impede the development of unrestricted exchanges, dividing tlietn under the heads of physical obstacles, arising from geographical position fomented obstacles, such as mutual jealousies, ; political hv Governments ; and moral obstacles, engendered by iguorance, prejudice, and sectional privileges. The first class of impediments were being fast

diminished by railway, steam communication, and the electric telegraph. I he secoud would disappear under the to operatiou of inventions seemed destined ultimately convert Europe which into one nation. Mr. Olivcira, M I'., said he represented a very numerous committee in England, whose object it was to obtain a reduction measure upon foreign wines as a necessary of the duty of Free-trade ; and which he felt sure would lead to reciprocal reductions ol tariffs in the countries which prodused þÿwines as France, Spain, and Portugal Upon this particular subject the policy of recent Governments injurious to the revenue, which in England had been had been stationary for the last twenty-five years ; it promoted the use of spirit-drinking amongst the lower classes of the population, with many attendant evils ; and it certainly restricted our commercial relations with foreign countries.

We announce with satisfaction that the representations relative to the deportes of Cayenne have already led to the important result of issuing orders to all the seaports of France that none of those condemned to be transported thither shall be forwarded to that destination. ITALY. We read in a letter from Rimini of the 20th inst. : þÿ " Yesterday morning very serious apprehensions were entertained at Pesaro for the maintenance of public tranquillity. Three years ago the Roman Government laid a tax on merchants, shopkeepers, and artisans of every description. The tax was very onerous, and pressed heavily on the last two classes of the population. It was never collected at Pesaro, where the decree was regarded as a dead letter. Some days ago, however, the authorities issued a proclamation calling on the merchants, and artisans to pay the amount of the tax for 1856, together with the arrears of the preceding years, threatening the refractory citizens with the withdrawal of their licenses. On Thursday last the collectors presented themselves in the different establishments, to levy the tax, but met everywhere with a refusal to pay it. The next day all the shops throughout the town were closed, and the population tilled the streets. The authorities, alarmed at the demonstration, had stationed a detainment of Swiss troops on the square, in the hope of intimidating the people ; but the latter offering a mere passive resistance, and committing no riotous acts, they withdrew the troops about noon, and caused a notice to be posted up in the different quarters announcing that the payment of the tax was suspended. The shops were then re-opened, and the town resumed its usual aspect." The Pope has received from the Emperor of the jBtirmans rich presents brought

to him by a missionary. Those presents consist of a chalice of solid gold, a cross enriched with precious stones, and valuable rings, accompanied by a letter in which the Catholics inhabiting the Barman empire convey to the chief of the Church the expression of their affectionate attachment. The cardinals and prelates belonging to the Congregation of Extraordinary Catholic affairs had lately met at Rome to consider various questions connected with the religious affairs in the East. The Sultan, it appears, had made propositions to the Holy See, through the medium of Monsignor Hassoun, Latin archbishop of Constantinople, to the effect of establishing diplomatic relations with Rome, which would be extremely advantageous to the Catholics of the Ottoman empire.

THE DISPUTE WITH RUSSIA. The question of the Isle of Serpents is not yet settled, in spite of all that has been said to tbat effect. According to late despatches from

ST,, G R 0 lj X AVIS St. Petersburg, Russia intends to prosecute her claims to the rock, and is using every effort to induce other Powers to make it a subject for mutual decision. There ought to be no qucs tion whatever that the Island of Serpents has traditionally belonged to the Power which holds the nearest continental land. The new Russian frontier, though extending beyond the Dneister, will make Russian ground at least fifty miles from the Island of Serpents, whilst it is within about twenty of the mouths of the Danube. That fact alone ought to settle the dispute. Our naval force has very positive orders should Russian troops again attempt to land.

Night Scene in a Young Lady's Bedchamber. þÿ Last Tuesday night, which will be remembered as one of the warmest of the season, a young lady at the " Westend" was excessively frightened at a little circumstance which transpired about the hour of midnight. The young ladv, whose beauty is only equalled by her modesty, and whose þÿ eye's dark charm" has caused more than oue waistcoat to palpitate, had retired to her chamber, when, after laying aside the greater portion of her wearing apparel, she committed herself to the tender embraces of Morpheus, whose soothing influences were aided by the cooling breath of Zephyr, who came in at the open window and fanned her cheeks with his feathery wings. Tn a word, she was snoozing finely. It was about midnight, when the young lady was roused from her delicious slumber by hearing a noise at the window . Half unclosing her eyes, she was startled by the sight of a corpulent form, apparently struggling to gain admission to her chamber through the open window. It struck her at once that the intruder had been caught by the rear of his unmentionables by a nail or some other sharp instrument, as he seemed struggling with a stern determination to enter. Her first thought was to faint, her second to give the fellow a push, her third to jump out of the window as soon as he jumped in, her fourth to immediately carried into effect. The w histle of the locomotive on the Iron Mountain road, when it gave its first snort on the 4th of July, was but a

whisper to the scream of the young girl. The whole house, and half the neighbourhood, ware awakened by the cry. The old folks, three female servants, and two big brothers rushed to the rescue, and broomsticks, mop-handles, and bootjacks flashed as the household entered the chamber of the frightened beauty. An examination of the figure in the window dispelled the tear> of all, and changed the screams laughter. of the young lady into shouts ol The imaginary " fat man" was only her own darling hooped skirt, which she had hung on a hook near the window, and which the w ind had inflated and set in motion. There was 110 more sleeping in the house that night. þÿ St. Ijiniis Heralit, August 1 1 .

| From the Illustrated Loudon News.) The American newspapers have brought intelligence of a rapture between England and Mexico. They state that our Minister there has demanded his passports, and sent for an English squadron to blockade the Mexican ports. There must, we presume, he some axaggeration in this, as it is tantamount to a declaration of war against a State which has of late been on very friendly terms with us, and which, from having been, unfortunately for some years, involved in political convulsions, merits from us consideration and forbearance. Having got through its troubles, Mexico is settling down into tranquillity and order under its present Government, and is now, we see by a late Mexican journal, intent on securing for itself, as the great step to future progress and welfare, perfect religious toleration. No envoy of her Majesty would venture, we hope, to commit the country to a war against such a State without an urgent necessity, such as we cannot believe has arisen, while the public is left in total ignorance of the whole matter in dispute. Unfortunately, the loss of the Toy, which was charged to bring the mail from Vera Cruz, has prevented authentic information from reaching this country by the usual channel; and ifsuch information he in possession of the Foreign office, it has not been made known. As Parliament is not sitting, it is optional with the Foreign Secretary to withhold from the public, till the evil he consummated, the reasons for assailing and weakening a nation that may be

a useful political ally and a commercial friend. We happen, however, to possess some little knowledge on the subject, and the following, we believe, will prove to be a correct outline of the matter in dispute. Some twenty or more years ago a Mr. Barron, an Englishman, who had served in it Spanish army sent against Peru, left that service, and established a mercantile house at Teipic and San Bias, in the province of Jalisco on the western coast of Mexico. lie acquired some fortune and fame, and in December last year was carrying on his business there, having as partners it Mr. Forbes and his own son, who was also her Majesty's Consul for Teipic and San Bias. At that time Mexico was a prey to civil broils, and Messrs. Barron and Forbes were accused by the inhabitants ofTeipic and San Bias of having fomented disturbances and been very active on the side which was not successful. Special facts were alleged against them as occurring on December 13th. We know not the truth, but the people of these towns accused them very stoutly of contravening both the municipal and the fiscal laws of Mexico. In January last they presented a petition, very numerously signed and strongly reasoned, to Senor l>. Santos Pegollado, the Governor of Jalisco, stating these asserted facts, complaining bitterly of the conduct of Mrssrs. Barron and Forbes, and praying that the Governor would send Mr. Forbes out of the country as a "pernicious foreigner," and withdraw the exequator from Mr. Barron, junior, who, they

alleged, had abused his Consular power for the protection of fraud. Complying with the prayer of the petition, Senor Degollado excluded Mr. Forbes from the province, and refused to acknowledge the younger Mr Barron as her Majesty's Consul, breaking up their establishment and causing them considerable injury. Perhaps this was not

S T . C R 0 I X A V Ij S þÿ done according to law ; the petition might be considered as a private denunciation 011 which the Governor ought not to have acted; but some allowance must be made tor a people and their rulers embroiled in civil contests. It was imputed to the Englishmen that they supported with great zeal the unsuccessful cause ; and if they really sided with one party they might expect the animosity of the other. Strong, however, in their rectitude, and in the support of her Majesty's Minister in Mexico, Messrs. Barron and Forbes carried their case before the general Government, and made demands tor redress. Mr. Lettsen, her Majesty's Charge d' Affaires at Mexico, siding entirely with them, insists, it is said, on Senor Degollado being severely punished for his conduct, while Governor of Jalisco, towards those gentlemen, and that there shall be paid to them as compensation for the injuries they have suffered the sum of two million dollars. On the Government, after some negotiation, refusing to comply with his requisition, Mr. Lettsen has demanded his passports, and has ordered, it is said, her Majesty's ships to blockade the coast of Mexico. We give this brief version of the dispute as it has reached us, but we are too imperfectly informed of all the details to offer any opinion 011 the merits of the case. While on the one hand it is the duty of the Government to protect all her Majesty's subjects to the utmost of its power from personal injury or spoliation, it is also its duty to take care

that its power is not abused by its agents, and that British subjects under its protection do not mingle in civil broils in other States. Our Government undertakes to give effect to the fiscal laws of China, and it would be very inconsistent were it to lend its power to protect the violators of the tiscal and municipal laws of Mexico. We remember with some shame the enormous claims of Don l'acitico, enforced by an English tleet against the Government of Greece ; and we are always apprehensive that all claims made 011 feeble States by individuals who suppose that they can get our Government to back their demau Is may be equally unfounded. Before such cases be made the. justification lor putting fleets in motion, impeding trade, and running the risk of involving us in further quarrels, they ought to be submitted to some mixed commission or impartial tribunal. Diplomatists are always commissioned to take a side, they are bound to stand up for the supposed power and honour ofthe country which commissions them, and are generally wanting in the impartiality which is proper to a judge.

Russian Projects. þÿ Advices from St. Petersburg furnish the details of the recent subsidies granted by the Russian Government for the formation of steam companies in the Black Sea and elsewhere!. They will amount annually to between 400,000/. and 500,000/., the line to Alexandria alone receiving 50,000/., besides other privileges. The total capital to be employed is200,000/., and the shares, which were all taken up immediately, now command 10 premium. The vessels are all to be built to carry guns, if necessary," and the movement " is regarded by many as a clever mode of creating and maintaining a navy so as to evade the Treaty of Paris. Some ofthe lines, it is observed, are obviously such as never could have been formed for legitimate purposes of trade : and the cry is thai Russia

will now get effective ships lor political purposes at a cheaper rate than if they were avowedly in Government service. The same advices mention that the late statement in Le Nord ofthe concession for the proposed network of Russian railways having been finally granted to the Paris Credit Mobilier, Messrs. Baring, and others, was incorrect, or at least premature.

Critics. þÿ Critics are a race of scholars, always esteemed like brokers, who, having no stock of their own, set up a trade with that of other men ; raking into sligiil wounds where they find any, or scratching till they make some where there were none before. The eye of a critic is often like a microscope, made so verv fine and nice that it discovers the atoms, grains, and minutest particles, without ever comprehending the whole, or discerning the general harmony.

THREE RULES FOR BORROWERS. 1. Never borrow a newspaper, book, umbrella, horse, or anything else whatever, if you can possibly do without it ; and not even then, unless with the previous cheerful consent ofthe owner. 2. Use the article borrowed more carefully than if it were your own ; and do not retain it beyond the time agreed on, unless with the owner's consent. 3. As soon as you have done using the thing borrowed return it, with thanks, until you can return the favor.

Romance. þÿ A little grain of romance is no ill ingredient to preserve and exalt the dignity of humane nature, without which it is apt to degenerate into everything that is sordid, vicious, and low. Suspicion. þÿ There are cases in which a man would be ashamed not to have been imposed on; there is a confidence necessary to human intercourse, and without which men arc more injured by their suspicions than they would he by the perfidy ol others. Humility is a flower that prospers most when planted on the rich soil of a noble and great, mind. Liberality is the best way to gain affection : for we are assured of their friendship to whom we arc obliged. Till", kindnesses of a friend lie deep ; and. whether present or absent, as occasion serves, lie is solicitous about our concerns. It is no flattery to give a friend a due character ; for commendation is as much the duty of a friend as reprehension. We should choose a friend endued with virtue, as a tiling in itself lovely and desirable ; which consists in n sweet and obliging temper of mind, and a lively readiness in doing good offices

St. Thomas, 1st November, 1856. To the Editor of the St. Croix " Avis." My Dear Sir, Permit me to solicit the insertion of the following article in your valuable paper as soon as it may be in your power : þÿ 1. Whatever subjects may be transmitted to you for the purpose of insertion, which may be construed as of an accusing or grossly vituperative nature are generally to be avoided, especially when such subjects may be, thus strictly qualified. 2. We, bold that articles of a libellous nature are those in which truth and falsehood arc blended ; 2ndly, when they treat of subjects which are entirely false without possessing one grain or atom of truth ; and lastly, when accusations reach to such a preponderating degree that truth is overwhelmned and hardly manifests itself through the venomous shafts of calumny and misrepresentation. 3. The just sense of mankind has ever held such Reptilism in abhorrence ; and the Laws which have been promulgated against this abuse condemn with reason, individuals thus guilty of calumny, to such degree of punishment as may correspond to the gravity of the case. 4. But if this species of Reptilism be condemnable as emanating from a solemn abnegation of Truth, ought Truth itself therefore not to he spoken ? If Truth be disagreeable to the originators, abettors, or participators of iniquity, will it not find favor in the bosoms of the just and the upright !

S T . C R 0 I X AVIS . 5. When it is said that Virtue is the Child of God, and Truth is her handmaid; þÿ shall we blench from the helm when the winds are highest and calamity threatens us ? No ! let us do no such thing, but manfully oppose every obstacle which may present itself to stop the dissemination of the principles of truth and justice. 6. How many things are submitted to in silence by the public þÿ not because of their insensibility þÿ not because they are not recognizable or that they are unknown : on the contrary, they are well known and properly understood ! ! Tis because any representation of grievance falls like a pointless arrow far short of its mark. What is and what must be the result ? Walker, been constituted a citizen of Nicaragua, and who is charged by that functionary, with the exchange of ratifications of the Commercial Treaty between the U. S. and Nicaragua, which was ratified bv the U. S. Senate at the late session. We learn from Major Ileiss some important particulars in regard to the itnpending conflict the between Walker and combined the forces of Gen. army of the Leonistas and the hostile States of San Salvador and Guatemala. The hostile forces were at Massaya, a town nine miles from Granada, and number at least twenty five hundred ; hut they are chiefly natives, said to he impressed into the service, and who are expected to desert upon the first opportunity. They have some artillery aud were preparing to attack Walker at Granada. The feuds of the several factions which compose the patriot party, had exfurther delay might pedited the preparations have for attack ; tor been attended with disorganization and dispersion. Walker's force at Granada numbered twelve hundred men, and was about to be increased by the reinforcements from Calitornia and New York, amounting to about four hundred. The New York companies had taken with them howitzers and mortars ; aud by the last steamer some rockets were also carried out. 1 hese and otliei munitions ot war destined lor Walkers service, are now, it is to he observed, regular-

ly passed through the New York Custom house. General Walker is said to he very desirous that the enemy should attack hint at Granada, which place is easily to he defended. We are told, however, that he will not wait for an attack after having received his reinforcements and artillery, hut will immediately march against the enemy at Masaya. There would be urgent reason for this course if the enemy should attempt to cut oil' his communications and supplies. A large British naval force, a list ol which we have already published, lies ofl" San Juan, and the officers ot the squadron were compelled to watch their crews very closely, in order to prevent their desertion to Walker, with whose cause they are said to sympathise. Too much credit cannot be given to the officers of the British squadron for their voluntary and official aid in the Texas out of the mud, near getting the entrance into the port, where she was stuck fast. The channel is shifting and had become Idled with mud so that the steamer draw- 11 feet of water, was stuck in the mud to the depth of -r> feet, and lay there perfectly helpless. Her situation being by the British squadron, several perceived vessels and their boats, with a large complement of men, were despatched to her relief. They attached t heir own hawsers to the steamer, main force fastened and hard by heavy tor and by pulling anchors, twentyfour hours continuously, set the Texas afloat. As the Texas passed near the squadron, her passengers and crew gave nine
hearty cheers, which were responded to from the men-of-war with the utmost cordiality.

MONTENEGRO. A letter from Vienna of the 7th, in the ( onslilulionncl , 1 says : þÿ " The reports which reach our War Department state that the number of Ottoman troops is increasing on the frontiers of Montenegro in such proportion as to give to Austria herself some right to take umbrage ; and besides, it is known that it is the best battalions of bis army which the Sultan proposes to employ against the Montenegrins, if war should break out. Prince Danilo, on his part, is redoubling activity in presence of the danger which seems to menace him, and by his order all valid men of from 20 to 50 years of age have been armed. Our officers who know the country estimate that the Prince could in the space of five or six weeks concentrate on the Turkish frontiers nearly 50,000 combatants. Although the geographical situation is different, our frontiers towards Montenegro may be compared to those of the two Danubian Principalities. Our statesmen, in common with the enlightened part of the nation, understand how important it is to Austria to exercise, even at the expense of Turkey, a high preponderance in Montenegro and in the two Principalities ; our political and material interests imperatively require it, and it is towards that object that since the commencement of the Eastern war all the efforts of our Government have tended. The relations

ST. CROIX AVIS. between our military commanders and Prince Danilo are as active and friendly as they possibly could be. Instead of endeavouring to thwart his pretensions to extend bis frontiers towards Turkey, our interest inclines us to encourage them, for they are supposed to be based only on the national desire to strengthen his territorial positions, so as to be better able to protect them against the incursions of the armed tribes of Turkey. A colonel of the staff has accordingly just left for Cettinjen, in order to have a conference with the Prince on the subject of the extension and fixing of the new frontiers of Montenegro."

The Italians in New York, as well as those who sympathise for Sardinia in her present struggle against Austria, have opened a voluntary subscription to contribute towards defraying the expenses for one hundred cannons, to be presented to the Sardinian people, for arming the new fortress on the mint of erection at Alexandria in Piedmont. It will be recollected that Sardinia is the only free government in Italy; there is freedom of the press þÿ there found shelter all the political exiles of other Italian Statesþÿ there the Bible is permitted to be circulated, and the citizens enjoy civil and religious liberty; and for this Sardinia has been denounced by the Pope. That small State although surrounded by despotic powers, has taken the lead for emancipating the whole Italian peninsula. As Austria has already advanced an army towards its frontiers, Sardinia will soon be compelled to meet the enemy in the open field, and from the result of the struggle will Italy rise from her political and national grave, or be doomed forever. The Banking House of G. Valerio & Co., L9 William street, New York, has already opened a subscription list for this purpose. All those who might be willing to take part in this legal demonstration in favor of Italy, may send their contributions to the above-named firm, or to the office of the Crusader. The same list of contributions has been opened in England, and even in the North of Ireland. Let it be said that the people
of the United States sympathise, not merely by words, but by acts with unhappy Italy.

The English people will not believe that his Majesty the Emperor of the French was cognisant ot the article in the Moniteur prior to its publication, that he approved of it afterwards, o. that he entertains auy alarm of or displeasure against the English press for their comments upon his domestic or foreign policy The writers of the English press honour him as one of the most remarkable men of his age. They see in hitu the eleet of the people of France, and one who has conferred new lustre on the great name he bears. They recognise to the fullest extent Ids transcendent abilities, and wish stability to his throne and dynasty, for his own sake, :or the sake of the people who have elected him, for the sake of the Anglo-French alliance, and for the sake of the peace and prosperity of the world. Rut, while admitting and feeling all this, and much more, the English press cannot abdicate its functions, and cease to comment upon the affairs of France with the same bo'dness and freedom with which it comments upon those of Great Britain. France is not Japan, or a remote island in the South Sea. If it were, the English press might be voluntarily tongue-tied with regard to its ruler and its affairs. France is a country within sight of our own shores, and is united with us in policy, as well as in commercial intercourse- What concerns France concants England -What endangers the credit of the one imperils the credit of the other. It is because the alliance is so intimate that public

opinion in this country declares itself so freely on all matters ot interest it: France- And if those who stand about the person of the Emperor would endeavour to understand the manners, the traditions, the feelings, and the impulses of Englishmen a little better, they would save themselves and their Imperial master from such mistak -s as t lie article in the Moniteur , and from many annoyances of more importance- What would tl'.ps,- people say if the English Government were to issue an announcement to the Emperor Napoleon declaring to him that the absence of a free press in France was a source of danger to tiie alliance? We have received letters front Vera Cruz setting tortli the fear which is entertained there that the British fleet will soon make its appearance off San Juan de Ulloa. The papers have also caught the swelling breeze, and the conjecture seems to be getting general. Something like a month ago we said such an advent might he expected. No one here can possibly form a correct opinion on the subject. Thus far the orders ol Admiral Fanshawe are unknown in Mexico, and the chances are at least even that the last of next week will see a hostile fleet in the harbor of Vera Cruz. The chances, we say, are about equal for further diplomatic parley or for immediate action. The whole character of the correspondence between England and Mexico on the subject of the present disagreement would justify the tears that are now so generally entertained, and Lord Clarendon's nhsencp front his office would also lead to the conclusion that definite orders had been forwarded to the Admiral. Rut what if defi-

T . & i 0 l X, A V I S , nite orders have been received and the Admiral makes his appearance at Vera Cruz ? Does any one suppose that he will set to work tiring shells into the city or even blockading the ports without any correspondence V Is any one so foolish as to fear that England will do a precipitate act? Supposing the fleet does make its appearance, England will only send her agent here to demand justice, and that justice cannot be denied. Mexico cannot lose anything by agreeing with England in this request, but what that justice shall be England will not dictate, if Mexico be disposed to settle the matter by a prompt and open discussion. It may not be agreeable to the pride of the nation to have such apparently coercive measures thrust upon it ; but England knows well the difficulties and trials through which the present government has passed, and is still passing, and will act with that leniency which characterizes an intelligent and powerful nation. The blockade of the ports of a nation which has no fleet would not be a victory ; to destroy her own commerce with Mexico would be wild madness. We are glad to see the Mexcan press taking hold of this matter in a proper manner. To our notions, there is far more advautage to be derived from calmly considering the threatening condition of the relations with England, than in calumniating the character of a pure and patriotic gentleman, who is charged with the settlement of the difficulty between the two countries. It will be remembered that we published, a few days ago, an account of the Mexican war steamer Domocrat being run oft' from Vera Cruz by her crew ; her subsequently appearing at the port of Coatzacoalcos and forcibly carrying off the collector tit that place, together with the customs specie in his hands, and the departure of the other Mexican war steamer Guerrero, front Vera Cruz, in search of the mutineers and their vessel. A passenger on the schooner Joven Maria, which vessel arrived here on Wednesday from Tampico via Campeachy, with specie, relates that when they arrived at the latter port the Democrat was there waiting the return of a boat that had been sent ashore with the Coatzacoalcos collector. On the departure of the Joveu Maria from Campeachy, the steamer Democrat started to sea, apparently in pursuit of the schooner; but not far out the latter met the Guerrero, still in search of the Democrat. They encountered, and its the schooner sped on her way from the scene her crew could distinctly perceive the two vessels engaged in deadly conflict þÿ seeing the flashing of the guns and bearing their report. The next arrival from Campeachy or Vera Cruz will doubtless bring us news of the issue of the fight between the mutineers and their former comrades. The Democrat, while at < 'oatzacoalcos, fired into and sunk a Mexican war steamer, - name unknown, formerly the American steamer Ren Franklin.

POLITICAL SAGACITY When the New York Herald first took up the cause of Fremont, the movement was con sidered a hoax. It was one of Bennett's amusing and funny caprices to attract atten tion. The idea of the Herald going for Fremont, without a party, and against two such old campaigners as Fillmore and Buchanan, was so very ridiculous that the democracy chuckled over it as the best joke of the season. The joke was particularly refreshing, after the Herald had taken so much trouble to prove to the democracy that Mr. Buchanan was their only man that could possibly carry Pensylva nia. A week or two after Fremont's nuuiina tion it began to he visible to the naked eye that the Herald was in earnest ; anil then it was discovered that Mariposa had done the business, and that" Bennett had been bought up, at various prices, ranging from one hundred to live hundred thousand dollars in California gold. With the Maine election, the democracy made the further discovery that Freemont was running like a whirlwind, and that if they did not look particularly sharp, and bring all their batteries to bear, he would certainly he elected. Now that the election is over, the\ discover, after the most prodigious efforts were made bv a desperate and unscrupulous party, and with all the aid afforded bv Fillmore, that Mr Buchanan is saved by about a dozen electoral votes. The election of James Buchanan to the Presidency of the United States for four years from the 4th of March next, is now placed beyond a doubt. He is elected by the people, and by a handsome majority. In short, the triumph is complete, in every department of the national government. Sectionalism is defeated, and driven back into its den, abashed and confounded. The Union is preserved and strengthened. Patriotic men may now breathe freely, and business men can make their calculations safely, so far as domestic matters are concerned.

From the New York Herald, November 7 THE CABINET AND THE POLICY OF MR. BUCHANAN. We perceive that some of our democratic cotemporaries are already beginning to look up the necessary timber for a new Cabinet for Mr. Buchanan. It is not likely that he will retain a single stick of the ministry of poor Pierce, although it is said there is a strong personal attachment between Mr. Buchanan and old Mr. Marcy, the result of many years of harmonious feeling at the same democratic crib. For all this, we may as well resign ourselves to say good-bye to Marcy, knowing, as we do, that the leading secessionists and filibusters of the Ostein! plot will make his dismissal a sine qua mm. We conclude, therefore, that the Cabinet of Mr. Buchanan will be a new Cabinet, from beginning to end, and the work of compounding it will be a very nice, a very delicate and a very ticklish piece of business. We are opposed, and the bulk of the Northern people arc opposed, to any sectional war against slavery in the South, or against the slaveholders as a class. The Southern States form an important part of our common country þÿ their people are our people, arid we share in their prosperities and their reverses. But they must not be led astray by plotting traitors and disunionists þÿ they must rather be brought back to the constitution, to reason, and a spirit of conciliation and compromise. Let Mr. Buchanan look to this and he may command the support, of all sections ; let him fail, and his downfall will be speedier and more ignominious than that of poor Pierce.

J T, G B, 0 I I A VIS. TIIE RESULT OF THE PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION TO OUR FOREIGN POLICY. The election of Mr. Buchanan will full like a thunderclap on the European governments and people. The warmth with which the candidature of Col. Fremont was espoused by the independent public opinion of the United States had led them to conclude that an event which they had grave reasons to deprecate would have been averted. Ignorant of our party machinery, they regarded these indications as unniistakeable evidences of the popular will. And so they would have been had not treachery, inexperience, and the absence of an effective organization combined to defeat the noblest cause which has ever engaged the sympathies of honest men. Ofthe effect of the news of Mr. Buchanan's success on foreign interests we shall not be long before we have an opportunity of judging. We are much mistaken if the London and Paris money markets do not afford immediate evidence of the public feeling abroad on this subject, and it is pretty certain that the dock yards of Portsmouth and Charbourg will also betray unmistakeable indications of the light in which this event is viewed in higher quarters. These anticipations are indeed inevitable corollaries of our own action.

From the Herald, November c i. The News. With regard to the election, we have nothing to report to-day different from our announcement of yesterday. The domestic policy ofthe new administration already promises an excitement. Mr. Buchanan, it appears by our telegraphic despatch from Washington, has declared that he is in favor of the admission of Kansas as a free State. Now that he is elected he admits the necessity of this course. The South will be indignant, and efforts be made at an early day to obtain two new States from Texas to offset Kansas in the United States Senate.

Tiie Great Results and the Suggestive Developemems of the Presidential Election. The general results of this Presidential election in the North are of the most tremendous and imposing character. The democracy have secured the election of Buchanan by the skin of his teeth, and only through the silly divisions, defections and bad management of the opposition forces in the single State of Pennsylvania. They only wanted a change of some fifteen hundred votes, out of an aggregate of four hundred and twenty-three thousand, to secure Pennsylvania in October; and this would have given them not only Pennsylvania in November, (which would have been enough, with what he has, to elect Fremont), but it would also have rendered the opposition majority in New Jersey and : Indiana a unit, thus making a clean sweep ofthe North, from stem to stern in behalf of the young eagle of the Rocky Mountains. In spite of all these unfortunate individuals, but for the bad management of the old fogy Fremont committees in Pennsylvania, the triumphs of Fremont would have involved every State in which the constitutional rights of free speech and a free press were not trampled under foot. It is not wonderful that with the results achieved by Fremont, the democracy are more alarmed than delighted with the election of Buchanan by the loss to the opposition of a single State. With the demands of the Southern secessionists on the one hand, and the results of the Presidential election in the Northern States on the
claim. " What am I, and what are the other hand, Mr. Buchanan may well exdemocratic party to do to be saved ?"

Political parties in the United States. þÿ We see that some of the journals which have supported Colonel Fremont are consoling themselves for their defeat by expatiating on " the strength shown by what they call the republican party," future to be achieved by the same " repub- and by prognosticating triumphs in the lican party." A little reflection may possibly save these persons some mortification hereafter. The persons who talk of the strength of the republican party, and expect it to remain where it is, like Trinity Church steeple, or still better, to grow like a crop of wheat, may find themselves awfully mistaken some day. The large popular vote polled for Fremont was a thing of the moment ; a finite event, without preface or sequel ; it may serve to teach philosophy, but those who expect to use it as a basis for future political edifices, will come to trouble. Each Presidential election must be fought on its own basis; in each one, henceforth, there will be two main parties þÿ the conservatives and the reformers ; and it is reasonable to expect that on some occasions the latter will prevail. But to discount 1860 in favor of a "republican party," because the Northern masses rallied to the side of Fremont, is as unwise as it was for poor Fillmore to expect to be President. Next year, if the republican leaders go to the polls with their party, they will probably find it greatly diminished in strength. They can only hope to meet it again, if they rally, in 1860, once more

under the name of Fremont. The Name of Fremont. þÿ The magnificent run which Fremont has made in his first trial for the Presidency, appears to be rekindling at once the flame of his popularity. By several public meetings in this city he has been proclaimed their candidate for I860; and we have no doubt that all the Republican presses of New England are in his favor. Very well. Let us take things coolly and deliberately; and by the year of grace 1860 we may lie enabled to show the difference between F remont. and Fillmore in the South.

Printers vs. Orators. Compare the Orator with the newspaper, and we gain a taint glimpse of the ubiquitous power of the latter. The orator speaks to a few hundreds or thousands þÿ the newspaper addresses its million of millions. The words of the orator may die on the air þÿ the language of the newspaper is stamped upon tables as imperishable as marble. The arguments ofthe orator may follow each other so rapidly that a majority of his hearers may struggle in a net of ratiocination þÿ the reading of a newspaper may be scanned at leisure, without a tear of perplexity. The passion of an orator inflames the whole assembly þÿ the feeling of the newspaper sways the continent. The orator is for an edifice þÿ the newspaper is for the world ; the one shines for an hour, the other for all time. The orator may be compared to lightning, which flashes over a valley for a moment only, leaving it again in darkness þÿ the newspaper to a sun blazing over a whole earth, " and fixed on the basis of its own eternity " Printing has been happily defined " the art which preserves all arts." Printing makes the orator more than the orator. It catches up his dying words, and breathes into them the breath of life. It is the speaking gallery through which the orator thunders forth in the years of ages. He leans from the tomb over the cradle of the rising generation.

GREAT PEDESTRIAN FEAT. but better known as the " Aimnersmish Paddy Hoofs, the celebrated pedestrian, Antelope," is still carrying on his Herculean feet of walking round a lady in full dress 100 times in 100 consecutive days. He is now in his second week, and looks as fresh as when he first started. There are bets t<» a considerable amount that Paddy will never be able to accomplish his arduous undertaking. What makes it the more difficult is the tiict, that a fresh lady is substituted every day. It hits been observed that the dresses of these various ladies, instead of decreasing are also getting bigger and bigger almost every week. What the size, therefore will be before the 90th, much less the 100th, day is completed, the most elastic imagination snaps, like an overstretched piece of india-rubber, in its vain efforts to comprehend. It is also feared that there will he no open space large enough in the vicinity of the metropolis to admit of the experiment, as soon as it has expanded to its fullest dimensions, being fairly tried. In the meantime, however, Paddy displays uncommon pluck. His unfailing good humour, and cheerfulness under his trying labours, such as would exhaust the oldest and worst-paid postman of St. Martin's-le-Grand, win smiles of approval even from his fairest ramparts. We wish the brave fellow every success, and shall from week to week make a point, or or several points rather, of recording the onward march of his iron-tipped bluchers and undaunted perseverance. þÿ Punch.

SWEDEN. King Oscar opened the session of the Swedish Diet on the 23rd of October. In His Majesty's Speech we find the two following striking paragraphs on religious toleration and the rights of women : " An enlightened toleration tor the faith of others, based upon the love of one's neighbor and inspired by a conviction which lias become indomitable, constitutes the essence of the dogmas of the Protestant Church. It becomes a people whose King (iustaviis Adolphus, fought for great the freedom of thought and liberty of conscience, which lie sealed with his blood, to imitate his example and follow in his lootsteps. The ancient laws, which still impede the free exercise of public worship of every confession, must therefore be done away with, so that the common law muv be in harmony with the 16th paragraph of the Constitution. Bills for the abolition of the punishment of exile and for different reforms in the criminal code will be laid before you. " A just appreciation of the rights of woman being a sure guaranty of her in the fulfilment of her duties and fidelity of her mission in the family, it is my intention to propose to you that unmarried women shall be considered of age at 25, which is recognized in nearly all the States of Europe."

NAPLES, < >< t. 21. 1 have several times referred to the unusual activity exhibited of late tit the Ministry of Grace and Justice, and informed you that a Government return of those who have been amnestied was about to he published. It is now completed, and has been placed in the hands ot several ol the foreign Ministers. I have not been able to procure a sight ot it as yet, and must delay all details till some future occasion. This much I can communicate, however, upon very high authority, that it asserts t hat no fewer than 10,002 persons have been amnested since 1848. There are different a statement : First, the union in guilt of points of view þÿ from which to regard such so large a number must he taken as a fearful protest against some monstrous evil does that evil still exist? Secondly, assuming that the government ot this country were perfect and the King an angel, is the above statement a sufficient proot ot Royal compassion ? To ascertain this we must analyze the statement, which we are scarcely in a position to do. Still 1 am in- I formed that among the pardoned are battalions of the National Guard arrested on suspicion, or the national uniform þÿ from the mere men who laid down tact ot wearing that their arms in Calabria or Sicily, who had taken them up to defend a Constitution which had been promised to them on the Gospels, of and then laid crusaders promise pardon ; them down under from Lornhardy, who went forth with the Royal sanction, and came back many of them to

he beaten and sent to the islands in exile ; hordes swept away without any imputed crime, and sent off from their families on a earlino a-day to some distant place. According to the system of arrest which has been pursued during the last eight years, AO, 000 might have been amnestied without entitling the Sovereign to one grateful aspiration. But it would he interesting to know how many of those tried and condemned even by Neapolitan judges have been set at liberty. How innny are still in prison, what have been their sufferings, and what is now their position? Ilovv many are confined without trial by a simple misura di poliziu ? How many are in concealment, or wandering about leading a half bandit life? How many are in exile? and, lastly, how many are under the surveillance of the police? Could we make the calculation, should we not find another I (>,000 more waiting for the Royal mercy, altogether forming tt mighty protest against, a state of things real or imaginary which it would well become a heavenly-directed Sovereign to inquire into and correct ? It is not even now too late for the King to redeem the past. Neapolitans are a mild and forgiving race, and were His Majesty, under foreign guarantees against excesses, to restore the constitution, like a Christian man, jealous of his oath, his subjects would vet rally around him. Without an act ol justice as that tin amnesty is as useless as it would be impossible.

While the matter was being examined before a justice, the citizens broke into Court, dismissed the officers, and seized the prisoner and carrying him off bung him to a tree. þÿ þÿ > " þÿIt'll The " London Times," of the 29th Octobcr, contains the following remarks in reference to the President-elect, of the United States of America: þÿ Mr. Bi'chaxan lias been the most ductile and flexible of politicians. lie has been a Federalist and is now a Democrat, pro-Free Trade and anti-Free Trade, and pro and anti almost everything else about which parties in America have warmly disputed. He is not a man of great resolution or violent counsels, but lie possesses a peculiar facility of effacing himself and yielding

implicitly to the influence of those who surround him, often persons of inferior judgment to bis own. He is a thoroughpaced demagogue and unscrupulous partisan, and, in private grown gray among all manner of and niaiiieuvres. In this country we have not forgotten how adroitly he kept alive the quarrel with England which Lord Clarendon strove so earnestly to tenni-

countries in war, hut because lie saw, or fancied lie saw, from the continuance of 1 the dispute an electioneering advantage to himself. Europe has not forgotten the unseemly spectacle of the Congress of Ostend, when the representatives of America in Europe met together under the presidency of Mr. Sovle to bold a conference 011 the best manner of attacking the Governments of friendly States, and acquiring the lands of weaker Powers. The same principles which were laid down in that Congress by Mr. Buchanan and his associates have been embodied by the Democratic party in the Cincinnati platform, the manifesto under which they proposed to fight the Presidential campaign. From the conclusions of the Ostend Conference we extract the following, to show into

what hands the Government of the United States of America is perhaps in the very act of drifting : þÿ " Our past history forbids that we should acquire the Island of Cuba without the consent of Spain unless justified by the great law of self preservation. We must, at any rate, preserve our own conscious rectitude and self-respect. While pursuing this course we can afford to disregard the censures of the world, to which we bad been so often and so unjustly exposed. After we shall have offered Spain a price for Cuba far beyond its present value, and this shall have been refused, it will then be time to consider the question, does Cuba in the possession of Spain seriously endanger our internal peace and the existence of our cherished Union V This passage seems to need 110 comment. Its doctrines were not obscurely reiterated in the Cincinnati platform. To that platform Jlr. Buchanan gave his assent in these memorable words : þÿ " Being the re- " presentative of the great Democratic and not simply James Buchanan,

"the platform of that party, and insert 110 "new plank nor take one from it." This singular declaration has been the subject of much ridicule and comment in America. The press delight to remark that the Democratic candidate is no longer a man, but a platform, and have carried their irreverent mirth so far as to re-christen Mr. Buchanan, in true Yankee fashion, "James B. Platform." There are, as we have said, portions of Mr. Buchanan's character which would lead us to suppose that, although in assenting to the Cincinnati programme lie has nominally adopted as principles American ascendancy in the Gulf of Mexico and the unflinching application of the Mi nro doctrine, he will not be very forward to put these principles into execution. We may anticipate, also, that his accession to power as the representative ot the South will raise such a domestic commotion as will fully occupy his time and attention, without leaving him time to disturb the peace of his neighbours. This might well he if Mr. Buchanan could rule alone. But lie will be as much and probably more than ordinary Presidents a creature of his Cabinet, and lie will lie .surrounded by men who have the head to conceive and the hand to execute anv scheme that they believe beneficial to the party interests ot the South. To such persons as are the advisers of Mr. Pierce and will be the advisers of Mr. Buchanan foreign war is immeasurably preferable to domestic defeat, and the acquisition of a new Slave State, to oppose to the next free

territory from the north-west that may demand admission to the Union, is cheap at any expenditure ot blood and treasure. There are some civil discords that incline to peace, others that urge directly towards war. It remains to ho seen whether the furious commotions of Republican America be of the former or latter character. For England the course of policy marked out by events is clear and obvious. We cannot forbear sympathizing with the party which would check the extension bv armed force of the degrading and debilitating institution of slavery into countries unsuited for its operations and utterly hostile to its extension. But in the future President of the United States, whoever he may be, we recognize nothing hut t lie elected chief of a friendly Power. Whatever his antecedents, whatever his professions, we will persist in believing that the chief of the people of America will, when once elected, rise to the dignity of his position, and, casting off his more questionable antecedents, will know how to maintain at once the dignity of the Republic and the respect due to the feelings and interests of foreign and friendly Powers.

RUSSIA. A continental paper has published the following þÿ 1 : þÿ The letter, dated frontiers of Finland, November experience of the late war has opened the eyes of Russia to the iuadequacy of her coast defences, and shown how exposed are her frontiers iu Finland, and how open to any attack on the sea-board from hostile fleets. During the war the Governor-General of Finland, Couut Von Berg, was ordered to do his utmost to strengthen the existing coast defences, and send in plans for constructing uew naval fortresses in the province under his command. The subject engrossed the attention of the late Emperor of Russia, and his repented visits of inspection to the North are matters well known. Soon afterwards orders were given to build a strong fort ou the island of Kasko, iu the Gulf of Bothnia, commanding the entrance to a deep and spacious harbour, and destined to make good the loss experienced Gy the fall of Bomarsuud. All along this line of coast for a distance of 400 miles there were to fortified places. Brahestad, Uleaborg, Christinenstad, Lowis.i, Wasa and Karleby, were only commercial ports, and it is only at Hango Head and the neighbouring Guslawsvarn that any fortified works arc to found. Tn order to protect the coast lor the future, Russia has now decided on constructing five new fortresses, the preliminary arrangements lor which have been made this summer, and the ground marked out. One of these is situated in the extreme Northernly corner of the Gulf ol Bothnia, a very short distance from the frontier

town ofTornea. The selection of the locality appears to be well made and likely to answer the purpose for which it is intended- The river Lcmielf flows into the gulf at this spot, and the promontory of Sando-Saara, where the proposed batteries are erected, will sufficiently protect the entrance to a beautiful and spacious harbour. As the soil all about this place is favourable for agriculture, and there are roads communicating with all parts of the interior, it is proposed to lay out a new town, and by granting certain privileges and facilities, it is expected that many settlers will be þÿattracted. Letters from St. Petersburg state that Count do Morny is entirely occupied there in preparing the bases of a commercial treaty between France and Russia, by which French commerce will obtain important advantages for the entry of its productions into the Russian territory. It is well known that French merchandize, particularly millinery and fancy articles, is in groat favour in Russia, but is loaded with such heavy import duties that the price is doubled and often tripled. The consequence is, that large quantities are smuggled in, to the prejudice of the regular trader- The new Russian tariff, by diminishing the customs duties, will do away in a great measure with the smuggling trade, and the result will, at the same time, be an improvement in the revenue for the Imperial treasury, and fresh advantages for French dealers.

Charles XII. had none of the virtues of his predecessors, except their courage, but be will ever be remembered as the hero of romance, and uiore painfully for that fatal defeat of Pultawa, which laid the foundations of the power which Russia has ever since exercised over Europe It is trite to remark on the vicissitudes of nations or of individuals, but in reference to the fierce struggle of the North, where so many different peoples have striven fur supremacy, it may be here permissible to mention that the Swedes were once masters of Narva aud Novogorod, and the l'oles, of Smolensko and Moscow ; and, what is still more remarkable, that the Wasili quarter, now one of the principal quarters of St. Petersburg, was once the property of a Swedish subaltern. The decliue of Sweden must be traced to Pultawa ; siuce that date her provinces have been successively the prey of Russian ambition, which threatens at some future period, unless precautionary measures are taken and rigorously enforced, to absorb into its colossal empire all the Scandinavian nations. The military strength of Russia was first revealed to itself by the defeat of Charles XII. Thenceforward it encroached on all its neighbours, both by arms and diplomacy ; and the repulse of Napoleon, followed by the encampment of the Cossacks in the Champs Elysees at Paris, warned Western Europe that its civilisation might be endangered by the barbarians of the north. Happily, however, Russia was not, and

is not, a naval Power of the highest class ; but that defect, well known to herself, she diligently sought to repair by constructing Sebastopol, with a view to dominate over the Euxine, seize the Dardanelles, and through those straits penetrate into the Mediterranean. That dream of ambition is now dissipated for many years to come, perhaps for ever ; but, while indulging in those hopes, Russia was also seeking to become mistress of the Baltic, that she might pass through the Sound into the German Ocean. As her ports in the Arctic Ocean arc shut up by icc during eight months in the year, Russia lias coveted a naval station on the shores of Norwegian Finutark, where the mean temperature in the month of January ranges at 29 dcg. Fahrenheit. Such a position is thus described by M- Lallcrstcdt : þÿ The richest of the valleys, the most important for strategical aud economical purposes (that on which the aims and hopes of the Russians arc bent) is the vale of Alten, witli a river of the same name. Situated to the west of the Porsauger Fiord, this valley opens on the Alton Fiord, which, by its geographical position, offers astonishing resources for a first-class maritime establishment. This gulf has three entrances from the sea : Stiarsund on the west, Uognsund on the north, and Vurgsund on the cast. Each of these entrances leads to an excellent harbour, protected by its windings both from the winds aud the attacks of an enemy. No artificial defence is now raised on its shores ; no

strategic work lias yet been commenced there ; hut a lew advanced works would soon make it impregnable ; and if military engineers were called in, there would he soon raised around t his harbour a new Sebastopol, more dangerous and more solid than the first. Add to this that the vale of Alten þÿ rich, fertile, and well-peopled þÿ can supply all the materials and the labour necessary for a great enterprise. Alexander I. eagerly desired the possession of Fintnark ; aud it is highly probable that, had death not cut short his career of cupidity, lie would have seized it with strong hand, before Western Europe was aware of his designs ; lor he had picked a quarrel with Bernadotte, Ring of Sweden and Norway, who had offered to si ll old hulls of ships to the now republics of South America, and the Czar affected high indignation at this bargain with revolutionary Governments. The frivolity of this pretext for a declaration of war is the strongest proof that lie meditated an unjust aggression. The boundary between Norway and Russia was fixed under the Emperor Nicholas on the 14tli May, 1820 þÿ the river Jacob, running west of Kola, forming the line of frontier ; but he did not abandon the crafty tactics of his brother. In 1841 Russian emissaries, pretending to cultivate geology and botany, made a tour through Eastern Finmark. mapping down the course of the rivers, and the depth of covered by a Norwegian " who happened to re- water in the harbours ; but this plot was disceive a letter from a Russian official, the enve-
lope of which was formed, by mistake, of a frag-

ment of a circular addressed by some Russian authority to that same official." That circular contained uuuibered questions on all the localities aud capabilities of the qpuntry, with the view to construct a harbour fitted to receive and shelter a powerful naval armament. This alone is convincing proof of the secret machinations of lLu-.-. . ...id, ii 1 space permit, much additional evidence could be adduced. If Russia could thus establish herself in Fiumark she would become as formidable ou the ocean as she is on the land. " When Deter the Great." observes M. The liarhour of Alteu is now scarcely more known to statesmen than Azoff was in 1720. Once in possession of Alten the Russians would soon he lords of Norway, and have free access to the We-t. The seizure of Finland, and the rule to which it has boeu subjected, is an instructive lesson to those who credulously believe in Russian honour and Russian justice. The career ot Gustavus Adolphus IV., from his accession to the throne of Sweden, on the 1st November, 1796, to his forced abdication on the 13th March, 1S09, was marked by generous impuls s, rendered nugatory, and even ridiculous, by infirmity of purpose. We cannot here trace his mournful story ; but it was under his ill-fated reign that Finland was

lost, not by any brilliant achievement iu arms, but by imbecility, baseness, and corruption. Among the secret clauses of the Treaty of Tilsit, concealed from their own diplomatists by Napoleon and Alexander, the former yielded Kinlaud to the latter, and the Czar accepted the spoils of his brother-in-law, who had been his ally against the ruler of France. In this nefarious act. of spoliation, General Buxlioewden commanded the Russian forces. Ho was accompanied by a Swedish refugee General Baron Spungporteu, who hud sold himself to Russia, aud was willing to purchase the consciences of others as vile as himself. Colonel Jaegcrhorn was auother conspirator, aud one of the officers in command at Svcaborg, the military key of Finland. Sveaborg was built on seven rocks, and fortified by powerful works erected by Marshal Ehreuswaerd, which occupied twenty-five years iu their construction. It was defended by nine hundred guns and six thousand disciplined uud devoted tueu. Of the siege or sham siege, M. Lallerstedt gives the following account : þÿ " The command of this important place was confided to the Admiral Count Cronstedt; the siege was directed bv General Siiclitelen. It was expected that Sveaborg would be found to be impregnable, or at least that its reduction would cause the enemy a great loss of men and of time ; but against this difficulty the corrupting influence of Russia was called into play. False Swedish newspapers were printed and distributed among the soldiers and inhabitants of the

besieged town, announcing that 60,000 French troops had invaded .Scania and dethroned (iustavus Adolphus. In addition to these false statements to discourage pa riotism by direct bribery, appeal was made to treason. The following aro the most striking passages of the article which appeared in the Paris Constitutionnel on the question at issue between the English and French Governments : þÿ " The change of Ministry which has taken place at Constantinople is interpreted by some journals as a check experienced by our policy, and as destined to aggravate the difficulties which have arisen in that quarter. Too great haste has been displayed in giving to this event a signification which appears to us at least premature. Will the return of Redschid Pacha to office have for result to envenom a state of things which is already unsatisfactory, and to close the natural issue which is open for the difficulties that preoccupy Europe ! We hope that statesmen will comprehend the actual position of matters in a more favourable manner than appears to be anticipated, and that he will adopt the only line of conduct which is compatible with the honour and dignity of his country. Can Turkey consent to the presence of foreign forces on her territory when the proper period has passed away, when a plausible motive for this occupation no longer exists without abdicating all pride, without humbling herself in the eyes of the world ? What is only for the remainder of Europe an infraction ot treaties is a direct affront offered to Turkey. This Power has demanded the withdrawal of the English and Austrian forces, and it is for it a question of honour and vital interest to persevere in its demands. In fact, that

Power is more interested than any other in seeing that those clauses of the treaty are respected which have no other object than to guarantee its independence and safety. The misunderstandings to which the execution of the treaty of peace have given rise are open to the appreciation of the public ; every sincere and honest mind may decide upon their merits. The French press, with its diversity of opinions, has, to its honour, unanimously condemned the pretensions advanced by the Governments of Austria and England. Good faith and reason are, it is true, evident in the thesis maintained by the French Government. Article 20 of the treaty formally attributes to Russia the possession of Bolgrad in the new settlement of the frontiers. (' The new frontier will be traced from the Black Sea It will pass to the South of Bolgrad,' &c.) The text and the spirit of the treaty appear clear. England and Austria pretend, nevertheless, that in the idea of the Plenipotentiaries it was a question not of Bolgrad, a town of some importance, but of a simple hamlet likewise which is called Bolgrad. This is the difficulty that exists, and which Russia consents to submit, along with others of less importance, to the Congress, as was agreed upon ; she will defer to its decision 011 every point. What can be objected to this proposal V Is not this the solution recommended by good sense and good faith 1 Either it is sought to solve the question by means of an arrangement through an arbitration, or a fresh war is

desired. In the first case, what more satisfactory arbitration could be found than that of the very parties who contracted and concluded the treaty, the equitable interpretation of which is the source of the present dispute t Has not that case, moreover, been anticipated by the understanding that a new meeting of the Congress would take place in order to solve the questions which might remain open, and in order to assure the complete execution of the stipulations 1 Those who oppose the new Conferences create, therefore, at this moment, the only and real obstacle to the execution of the treaty. We arc told that

S T C R 0 |. X A, V Ij s the intention has been formed of occupying the seas and the provinces of the Turkish empire until all the stipulations have been accomplished. This policy is open to the most unsatisfactory interpretations. In fact, the presence of English naval force in the Black Sea, of Austrian troops in the Principalities, must henceforth be recognized as an arbitary and violent means of preventing the solution which Russia is wil- O g . ling to consent to, by proposing to submit the question to her natural judges. Will it be proposed to have recourse to force, to recommence the war ? Will the English Cabinet feel inclined to re-enter the lists, not certainly to assure the execution of the Treaty of Paris, but in order to tear it to pieces imprudently before the eyes of the world, with the view of satisfying an ambition momentarily disguised V" The Paris correspondent of the Times gives a few particulars of the birth, parentage, and education, of this semi-official manifesto : þÿ " I understand, that the article to which I call your attention is but a very modified form of that which was originally written, and which, I believe, was sent to the departments last night in the evening issue of the paper. When the persons under whose more immediate supervision the press is placed saw it they were somewhat startled, and suspended the issue until it was ascertained on what authority the article was published. The answer was that it had been suggested by the Foreigu-office, if not drawn up there. In-

quiry was made at the Foreign-office, and, I am told, the reply was, that though the hints or materials may have emanated from that official quarter, yet it was not intended to be so strong as the writer made it. It was then modified in its general tone and some of the harsher phrases removed ; and it was allowed to appear as it stands. The question now is, whether the article either in its present or in its former shape represents the true feelings of the Emperor as well as of the Foreign-office. I should hope not, as a few essays more of the same kind, considering the position of the French press, would go a good way to weaken the alliance between the countries."

Gn Tuesday last the 2nd instant I called with Mr. Sehou to look at the entries, on making it known to him, his answer was that he had not made a single entry in the hooks for the last month, and that he could not get them from Captain Golden. We could furnish, il need were, from our owti experience, a score of illustrations to prove the truth ot his remarks. In all branches of business, in all avocations, character, in the long run, is the best capital. Says Poor Richard: þÿ þÿ The sound of your hammer at five iu the morniug, or nine at night, heard by a creditor, makes him easy six months longer; but it lie sees billiard table, or hears your voice at you a tavern, at a when you should be at work, he seuds for his money the next þÿday. What is true of the young mechanic, is true also of the young merchant or the young lawyer Old and sagacious firms will not long continue to give credit for thousands of dollars, when they see the purchaser, it a young man, driving fast horses or hauging about drinking saloons. Clients will not entrust their cases to advocates however brilliant who frequent the card-table, the wine-party or the race-course. It is better, in beginning life, to secure a reputation for industry and than own houses or lands, it with them, probitv, you have no character- A facility of obtaining credit at the outset is often an injury instead of a benefit. It makes

the young beginner too venturesome, fills him with dreams of too early forture, tempts him too much to neglect hard work, forethought, caution and economy. Excessive capital is as frequently a snare to a young man. In lias almost passed into a proverb, in consequence, that the sons of rich men never make good business men. To succeed in life we must learn the value of money. But a superfluity ot means at the outset is nearly a certain method of rendering us insensible to its value. No man ever grew rich who had not learned and practised the adage þÿ If you take care of the pennies the dollars will take care of þÿthemselves. Knowledge of men, self-discipline, a thorough mastery of our pursuits, and other qualifications, which all persons of experience look for, are necessary to give the world security that a young mini is of the right metal. Capital may be lost, but character never Credit once gone the man without character fails. But he who has earned a reputation for capacity, integrity and economy, even if he loses his capital retains his credit, and rises triumphant over bankruptcy itself. A man with character can never be ruined. It is the first thing a young by every one who desires it in earnest A poor boy with character is more fortunate by far than a rich þÿman s s on without it

(From the Grenada Chronicle, November 29.J Barbados. þÿ We extract the following from the G lube's Packet Summary of the 27th ultimo : þÿ þÿ All interested in Barbados will learn with regret that the Island is about to lose the services of its Colonial S cretary, Mr. Walker, who will shortly leave, for an indefinite period, to resume the administration of tile government of Grenada, held by him since last May, and from which he had returned here on a brief leave of absence During his brief administration of the Government of Grenada, lie gained the golden opinions ol all classes; and with a prolonged opportunity of bringing his talents, bis energy, and bis intimate acquaintance with the requirements of the eoloni-ts into effect, we augur results highly beneficial to the interests of bis new Government ; whilst we greatly fear that Barbados will never again possess so able and so experienced a Colonial Secretary. þÿ On Monday afternoon the 17th. a great many persons of all classes, including Editors of Newspapers Medical Mon, Civil Engineers, Scientific Amateurs, and one Member of Council at least attended, by public invitation, to witness

certain expeiiinents in submarine blasting aback if the Refinery in Bay Street, by our enterprising fellow-citizen, Mr. John Inuiss: the operator was highly þÿsuccessful. The Barbadian newspaper signalizes last week as having been one of an unusually animated character to the religious world. There had been anniversary meetings of the West Indian Church Association for the furtherance of the Gospel in Western Africa, of the Wesleyan Missionary Society, and of the Moravians. His Excellency Governor Ilincks presided at the two first, and the Hon. Mr. Attorney-General Sealy at the last mentioned. We make room for a short notice of Mr. þÿSealy schairmanship at the þÿMoravians Meeting : þÿ þÿ He acknowledged that he had hesitated on being first asked to preside- He had never before co-operated with a religious body not of his own persuasion, and it. looked to him at first like a kink of desertion of his standard, to leave that portion of the army of þÿChrist Church s to which lie belonged, to fight under the banners of another portiou to which he did not belong. During twenty years ol publiu life he had carefully watched the efforts made to spread the softening and ameliorating influences of the Gospel among our still deeply degraded and deplorably ignorant

population, and he must say that the Moravians were second to none in those efforts. Does the English Minister seek to re enter the lists without France þÿ not, most assuredly, to ensure the execution of the hope that on this point, as well as regards the Treaty of Paris, but to imprudently tear it to pieces in the face of the world, with the object of satisfying ambitions momentarily disguised ?

We do not believe that the English people are prepared to ratify such a policy, and to cheerfully accept all its consequences. We willingly rely upon the good sense and the loyalty ol the English nation, and will accept them unhesitatingly as arbitrators in the difference ; for it is impossible to deceive them upon a question which unjust suspicions and the flimsiest sophistry have not yet been able to obscure The English uation knows the fidelity of their ally by a great and substantial proof, aud lias not cea ed to believe iu it. I he English nation knows that the Emperor Napoleon has not repudiated their alliance and that it is not to him that the reproach of incon fancy and versatility can be addressed. Certain journals, like the Times, not daring to come in direct collision with the great esteem of the English people for the Emperor Napoleon, imagine they can distinguish between the Sovereign and his Government the policy of the Emperor aud that of his Ministers. Such paltry subtleties need no refutation. They will fail to deceive any one in England ; and the Times has over-estimated the ignorance of its readers upon questions relating to our Governments U e repeat, ii depends to-day upon the Cabinets ot London and Vienna to put an end þÿ if that is what they wish þÿ to pending difficulties, and to the anxieties which this situation occasions. If we are well informed, despatches were sent off on the 31st October which will remove þÿa .l the partial difficullies that exist, which have moreover proceeded rather from subordinates than from the Govern meats themselves. The Treaty of the 30th March will be executed in all its rigour ; and afterwards, if Rus.-ia or any other Government wishes to submit questions to the Congress of Paris, the Congress will examine them with that spirit of progress beyond the range of which it is now impossible to effect anything in Europe that is destined to last.
