| From the Illustrated London News.) Who in the councils of the Emperor of the French is the traitor to the interests and cause ot' England, and to the Anglo- French alliance ? Where shall we look for the man who endeavours to sow disunion between his Imperial master and the Government of this country ? Who is the person, with Russian sympathies, and of Sclavonic origin and nameþÿ who, prior and subsequent to the signature of the hasty and ill-considered Treaty of Paris, has invariably used his iniluence and his abilities on behalf of Russian interests? Who is the Minister of France who endeavoured to destroy the liberty of the press in Belgium, and to a certain extent succeeded? Who is the man who hates free discussion in England, and tried, through the columns of the Moniteur, to bully the press which | he was unable either to bribe or coerce i There is but one man in the councils of the Emperor Napoleon to whom this description will apply, and that is M. Walewski, the Minister for Foreign Affairs. The attack upon this country, consequent upon the change of Ministry in Turkey, which, under the avowed auspices of the French Foreign-office, has been permitted to appear in the Constitutionnd , is only one proof amongst a hundred of the animus of M. Walewski, and of the feelings which he permits himself to entertain and to express with regard to an alliance which is the safety of France and the hope of Europe- Such an article in an English newspaper would signify nothing but the personal views of the writer ; but, in a French news-

paper, where no opinion can be expressed ! upon a political question without the sanetion of the Government, an article in a public journal assumes the significancy of j a diplomatic document. All who wish the I alliance of France and England to be cordial and permanent, must disapprove of the conduct of a Minister who, either wilfully or ignorantly, weakens or imperils via Savannah, to St. Thomas, Barbados, that alliance by his policy either towards England or towards Russia. It was no secret, even before the Constitutionnd, under the orders of M. Walewski, undertook to enlighten the world upon the subject, that there has been a misunderstanding between the British and French Governments on the question of the nonfulfilment by Russia of the stipulations of the Treaty of Paris. The bad faith of Russia is as patent now as her ruthless ambition was when her armies crossed the Pruth, and when her cowardly fleet destroyed the Turkish squadron at Sinope. Russia has quibbled understand his advertisement and prevaricated, and attempted, in defiance of the Treaty of Paris, to retain possession of Bolgrad and of the Island of Serpents þÿ stations that would give her the mastery of the Danube and of the Black Sea. France, under the influence of M. Walewski, who, it appears, is to receive from the ( Izar, as a reward of his zealous services, the confiscated Polish estates of his family, has insisted that these matters were of small moment. England, on the contrary, has insisted that they were of the and for the interest of the other Sharehold-

highest importance ; and that, rather than concede them to Russia, and so stultify itself in the eyes of the world, and prove that it had expended in vain its hard-earned treasure and the precious blood of one ot the noblest armies that ever fought in the cause of justice and independence, it, would

the good fight which it had left, unfinished. We cannot but believe that the Emperor of the French is, or will be, of the same opinion. It is the opinion, not only of the Government and people of England, but of Turkey the party most interested and the injudiciousness þÿ þÿ of Austria, which lias a vital interest in thi' freedom of the Danube. It is the

ST. CROIX Ai V I S opinion, we venture to assert, of all the .States and kingdoms of civilised Europe which are not under the influence of Russia. If the people of England could imagine for a moment that Napoleon III. was not thoroughly convinced of the policy and the necessity of holding Russia to the strictest fulfilment of the engagements she con- 1 tracted by the late treaty, the Anglo-French alliance would most indubitably be weakened. If that alliance is to continue, as we most fervently hope it will, there must be no truckling to Russia in this matter. France must support, by her words arid by her deeds, the same wise and courageous policy which led to the war, and which carried it through the glories of the Alma, and of Inkerman, to the final capture of Sebastopol. The British and French nations have learned to love each other from perils undergone and glory acquired in common. They are united by the strongest links of mutual self-interest, by social intercourse, by contiguity, and by a dailyincreasing commerce. Yet it would be idle to deny that, within the last few7 weeks, the English people have begun to look with more or less distrust upon the policy of the French Emperor and of the persons who form his Court and Cabinet. To restore the confidence of the English people there needs the dismissal of M. Walewski. As long as he continues to direct the ! Foreign Affairs of France, there is reason to fear that Russia will be emboldened to j break faith, England and France estranged,

Dueling. From tbo New York Journal of Commorco. The recent tragical occurrence in Charleston S. C., in which Mr. Taber, one of the editors of the Mercury in that city, was killed by E. Magrath, must not be allowed to pass away without a word of comment. It would be reasonable to suppose, that an event occurring under such melancholy circumstances, would startle the advocates of this criminal practise, and rouse the public from the apathy into which they too frequently settle upon this subject. The conductors of a public press admit to their columns an article hostile to the pretentions of a gentleman who has been announced as a candidate for Congress. The brother of the party who has been assailed in the communication, without inquiring for the author or attempting a refutation of the charges, proceeds at once to challenge the editor to mortal combat. The challenge is accepted. The result is that a gifted man is violently taken away, in the very prime of his days ; a father is carried to his home a mangled corpse ; a wife is bereaved, and children are made orphans. On the other hand, the challenger has infixed a stain upon his conscience which no tears can wipe away ; the memory of the deed will haunt him to his dying day. The sighs of a widow rendered wretched by the loss of a husband who has fallen by his hands, and the cries of bereaved children, must ring in his ears long after the public have forgotten the particulars of the tragedy. A system whose fruits are thus bad and only bad, bad tor the dead and bad for the

Packet desirous of knowing always my movements ; and for the interest of the other Shareholders, as well as myself, 1 deemed it wrong to cooperate with his wish, as thereby all lucrative trade would have been secured to said schooner, and the W. Packet, and which I stated in my notice of the 1st instant ; and the above paragraph further convinces the Public of the injudiciousness of electing the sole owner of another schooner to the Directorship of one owned by several Persons. THE ELECTIONS!!! Remember, Voters, to-morrow is Election Day ! Do not voluntarily remain away from the Poll, but go there and record your votes in favor of men whose interests are identical with your own, regardless of party-considerations or private influences ! This done, and you may secure the services of independent representatives in the Burgher Council, who will ascertain the real state of our circumstances, study its amelioration, and promote the true interests of the Island ! (Frotn the London Tinted, Dec. 4J. | The United States. From our own Correspondent.) NEW YORK, Nov. 20. Mr. Buchanan already begins to feel the discomforts of high station. What is to be the policy of the new-coming Administration is a question asked by the victorious party oftener and more pertinaciously than by the vanquished. Whether Northern or Southern þÿ Conservative or Fillibustering þÿ counsels are to Prevail ; whether Kansas is to be slave or free þÿ on all these matters the new President preserves a judicious silence, The Washing/on Union puts out an explanation of the Cincinnati Platform, which may be regarded rather as the dying legacy of Mr. Pierce than as a declaration on the part of Mr. Buchanan: þÿ " The Government of the United States has never interfered, and we feel assured will never interfere, with the internal affairs of Mexico or ( 'entral America, for any other purpose than that of counteracting the intrigues and en-

S T . C R 0 lj X, ft V I S , croachments of foreign Powers, and fostering their new-born freedom. With respect to Cuba the case is quite different ; nor do we think it will injure the reputation of Mr. Buchanan or any other American statesman, to be suspected of a desire to emancipate that fine Island from colonial vassalage, and (if such is the wish of the inhabitants) to admit it as a member of this confederation. It is not fit that the key to the Gulf of Mexico should be in the hands of an enemy, or one who is the mere tool of our enemies. The North and West, equally with the South, are deeply interested in this question, which seems to be sleeping now, but which, we opine, will never die." Virginia tor a " newspaper published, writ- Mr. Horace Greely lias been indicted in ten, and printed in the citv of New York, and styled the New York Tribune, with intent in him, the said Horace Greely, then and there to advise and incite negroes in the State of Virginia aforesaid to rebel and make insurrection, and to inculcate resistance to the rights of property of masters in their slaves."

From the Illustrated Loudon News. Nov. American" papers continue to give us the most remarkable reasons for being satisfied with t lie result of the recent election of the President, or rather of the President's electors. We are positively assured that those who form an unfavourable judgment of Mr. Buchanan, from his antecedents, do so upon unworthy premises. We may suppose that he endeavoured to keep up the quarrel between England and the States, but really he did no such thing, or, if he did, it was only to promote his election. We may object to the Ustend manifestation of annexation, but, though Mr. Buchanan signed that, he only did so to oblige the firebrand M. Soule, and had 110 hand in drawing it up. He is, moreover, an elderly man with a character to lose, and a docile man without much character, and an ambitious man with a character to win, and therefore it is not to be supposed that his policy will be that which is anticipated. Besides, he has always been favourable to making Kansas a Free State þÿ not a Slave State, and has said as much; and if he was not heard it was because the election riots drowned his voice. He could not, you know, be responsible for that. Putting all these things together, and they remind one a little of Archbishop Laud's " hundred black rabbits that did not make a black horse," we are requested to believe that Mr. Buchanan will be one of the best Presidents America ever had May it he so. In the meantime the South calls for more slaves, and a revival of the accursed traffic
of the
Merchants fraught with cargoes of despair while Mr. Walker is everywhere thanked, bv those who thanked Brooks, for having reintro duced slavery into Central America.

TIIE NEUFCll ATEI. QUESTION. The mission of General Dufour to the Emperor of the French is considered as a pledge that the Ncufchatcl question will be amicably solved. The general belief in Paris of is that, if the prisoners are released the King Prussia will not bo exacting as to the conditions under which his nominal sovereignty over the canton is to be acknowledged. It is said that, in accordance with the resolution of the Diet, Austria is to address a note to the Swiss Confederation, which is not to exclude representations from Bavaria and Baden. Among other rumours, it is affirmed that the Swiss people wish to have the question of the Royal sovereignty decided by the population of Neufchatel themselves; in fact, to appeal to universal suffrage. The Prussians say that his Majestv might try the experiment without any fear of the result, provided the suffrages of the Neufchatelois only were taken, but that lie would not admit the 24,000 or 25,000 who have for the last eight years poured into Neufchatel from Bertie, Valid, and other cantons. It was said lately that Baden, Wurtemberg, and Bavaria would allow the passage of Prussian troops in case the design of occupying Schaffhausen, attributed to the King, was carried into ett'cet ; hut this has been contradicted. Letters from St Petersburg say that Russia strongly upholds the claims of Prussia on Neufchatel. The Swiss Federal Council has submitted to our Govcrnmei t, and to all the other signitaries to the Treaty of London, an expose

framed to demonstrate that the demands made by Prussia are inadmissible in a. Swiss point of view, both in relation to the question of sovereignty and the setting the prisoners free without trial. The Russian Government has already made its reply, which persists in favouring Prussia, as might have been anticipated. The promptitude with which this reply was forwarded evidences the importance attached to the point that Switzerland should not remain in doubt as to the sentiments of Russia.

All that we can gather from the statement given is that a Russian cruiser from Abasia captured several Turkish boats laden with contraband salt ; that Admiral Lyons sent some gun-boats to ask the reason for this capture ; and that one of the boats (the Badger) having attempted to enter the Sea of Azotf, the Russians refused the passage through the Straits of Yenikale, and even fired upon the vessel.

Submarine Blasting. (From the Barbados Globe, Novr. 20.) We were present on Monday afternoon at Mr. Inniss's submarine blasting experiments, aback of the Refinery, Bay Street, which came off in the presence of a very large concourse of persons of all classes, who responded to the public invitation to be present. Mr. Inniss's object was clearly to demonstrate the very simple principle on which submarine blasting is now-a days conducted, and, but for the circumstance of his having had to extemporize for the occasion almost the entire apparatus used in making preparations for Monday after- noon's exhibition, we should say that it is blasting. not very wonderful that the operator was eminently successful. For the purposes of the experiment Mr. Inniss, as the best arrangement practicable (without incurring exorbitant expense) procured three large blocks of stone, between one and two tons

had sunk in seven feet water just at the extreme point of the Refinery Bridge þÿ this site having been chosen for the advantage of having the bridge as a platform to operate from. We need scarcely say that the end Mr. Inniss sought to establish by means of his experiments was his ability to perforate rock under water, charge it with gunpowder or other explosive material and explode the charge the power and force of the head. þÿ þÿ of the explosion depending of course on the quantity of explosive material employed. We have no time to go into the minute of the manner in which all the rocks were drilled ; but, as being enough for our present purpose, we will briefly explain sufficiently popular for information the modus operandi. A diving-bell, constructed of a Refiner's Baloon, (a cylindrical wrought iron vessel, 6 feet in diameter and 4i feet deep, rigged up with suitable gear) was lowered, through the flooring of the wharf, to within a few inches of one of the stones, which, displacing the water to within one foot of the surface to be operated upon, two men descended, and working comfortably for two-and-a-half hours, dril- ty led two chambers in the rock. The other blocks were drilled from the bridge, one with four, the other with two holes, the instrument employed being a fifteen feet iron bar, steeled at the end, passed through a pipe, placed steadily in position, and worked by two men who had only to lift the bar and let it fall, the hole being kept clear by the constant action of the drill. " Not the least attractive feature in the

preparations," writes a contemporary like ourselves, was present, " to most of who, the persons assembled on the occasion, was the Galvanic Battery, evidently of great power, which Mr. Cooper, Civil Engineer, had supplied for the occasion. This battery, we understand, was entirely constructed by Mr. Cooper himself of materials, with the exception of the zinc plates, procured in the island. The charges for the blasts, contained in tin canisters of only 3 ounces each, were being connected with the wires whilst the company to witness the experiments, were assembling ; and a little before 5 o'clock they were carried down into the water and fixed by divers into the chambers prepared for them. In about ten minutes after, everything having been fully arranged and the spectators warned of the approaching blast, the circuit was completed with the battery, and the resonance of the Bell, from the blast under it, with a puff or two of white smoke, and a slight ripple of the water over the other charges, told that the end had been attained. Borrowed Trifles The effects of Unbelief. þÿ Unbelief is the cause of all sin and the bond of iniquity. It does nothing but darken and destroy. It makes the world a moral desert, where 110 divine footsteps are heard þÿ where 110 angels descend and ascend þÿ where 110 living hand adorns the fields, feeds the fowls of heaven, or regulates events. Thus it makes nature, the garden of God, a mere automaton ; the history of Providence a fortuitous succession of events ; man a creature of accident ; and prayer a useless ceremony. It destroys the vestiges of heaven that remain upon earth, and stops the way to every higher region. Words. þÿ "Words, words, words ! " says Hamlet, disparagingly. þÿ Rut God preserve us from the destructive power of words ! There are words which can separate hearts sooner than sharp swords þÿ there are words whose stiug can remain in the heart through a whole year. þÿ Man/ Hoiritf. Good Things. þÿ Employ thyself" in something good. Do good to thy friend, that he may be more thv friend ; your enemy that he may become thy friend. 'Tis better to love to hear, than to love to speak. It is better to know many things than to he ignorant of all. Re a friend to virtue, a stranger to vice. Govern thy tongue. Learn to bear misfortune.

The London Gardeners'1 Chronicle lias the following remarks on the value of the Blue Gum Tree; it refers more particularly to Tasmania, but this Colony, especially the southern parts of it, can also furnish some splendid specimens of the tree : The readers of the Gardeners' Chronicle will not have forgotten the interest which attached to the specimens of timber from Tasmania exhibited in Hyde Parkin 1851. It was difficult to over-estimate the colonial value of that description of produce, whether for the purposes of naval construction, ordinary building uses, or cabinet work. Most especially was the magnitude of the Blue Gum Tree ( Eucalyptus globulus) a subject of universal wonder. We are, therefore, glad to have the opportunity of drawing attention once more to this mar- as vellous example of vegetable growth, described in the very ably written account of the Tasmanian contributions to the late Paris Exhibition, of which a copy has just reached us from its author, Mr. Milligan. It is true that Eucalypti are not trees for an English forest ; but we see no reason why they should not flourish in such climates as that of Killarney, as it is already known that they do on the once desolate island of Ascension. We copy Mr. Milligan's descriptions verbatim. With a plank exhibited by Captain Goldsmith, of Hobart Town, 70 feet long, 1 1 feet wide, and 3 inches thick, we have the following account: þÿ " This is perhaps the most valuable and important of the timber trees of Tasmania.

Its principal habitat is in the south side of the island ; but it is also met with in the valley of the Aysley and at the Douglas lliver, on the East Coast, and it reappears Upon Flinder's Island, in Bass's Straits ; its stronghold, however, is D'Entrecasteaux's Channel, and along the south side of the island, whence it has been exported in various shapes within the last three years to the value of about £800,000. The Blue Gum attains, when at maturity, an average elevation and size greater probably than any other tree in the world ; a plank forwarded to the London Exhibition of 1851, which, from the difficulty experienced in procuring a ship to carry it, arrived in England too late for exposition, measured 145 feet in length, and was 20 inches broad by 6 inches in thickness. A plank of the same width and thickness was cut 1(50 feet in length by Mr. James Boyd, Civil Commandment at Port Arthur, Van Dieinen's Land, in order to be forwarded to the Paris Exhibition of 1 855, but it has been found impracticable to get it shipped by any vessel at this port (Hobart Town), and it does not therefore appear in this catalogue. This tree attains at its full growth a height of 250 to 000 feet, and a circumference varying from 30 feet to upwards of 100 feet at 4 feet from the ground. In regular forest ground it rarely gives offits principal limb under 1 00 feet, and there is not unfrcqucntly a stem clear of any branch for 200 feet and upwards. The most important purpose for which this timber is adapted,

and to which it is extensively applied, is that of shipbuilding. The Messrs Degraves and Messrs Watson of this place have built and fitted out vessels with it, of which several are now trading regularly to and from England. Its specific gravity is greater than that of Teak, British Oak, or even Saul ; and experiments instituted to ascertain its breaking weight, &c., have established the fact, that in strength and elasticity it is superior to all other timbers.
